verdict: OK to lend in Pune auto OEM and its tier-1/tier-2 supply chain, but only against verified order books and with monthly stock and receivable reporting; avoid pure EV-bus startups riding subsidy and payment cycles.
title: Pune cars & commercial vehicles (OEM): a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**A Pune auto OEM or tier-1 supplier turns steel, castings, electronics and labour into vehicles or sub-assemblies, and gets paid weeks after the vehicle leaves the gate.** Cash sits in raw material and work-in-progress inventory, in receivables from the OEM, and in tooling and plant capex; the OEM holds pricing power, the supplier mostly does not. **So when a proposal lands, check who the end customer is and what share of the borrower's revenue that one OEM takes; if one buyer is above roughly half of sales, ask for the supply agreement and payment terms in writing.**

## What has changed now
**National output is running far ahead of the money lent against it.** IIP for NIC 29 is +25.2% YoY and +19.2% Apr-to-date [D], while bank credit to the sector is +27.0% YoY [D] — a +7.8 pp gap [D]. Maharashtra GST is +8.6% Apr-to-date against India +6.1% [D], so Pune's local demand is holding up. **Peer results are strong but margins are the soft spot:** M&M auto revenue +25% to ₹31,115 crore with EBIT margin 9.5% [5]; Tata Motors CV net profit ₹2,560 crore on volumes +26%, with commodity inflation prompting price hikes [6]; Q4FY26 auto EBITDA growth was seen at about 21% with commodity risk flagged [4]. **So when a proposal lands, check the borrower's gross margin trend over the last four quarters; if margins are falling while volumes rise, ask for the price-revision clause with the OEM.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue tier-1 and tier-2 suppliers with a confirmed purchase order from an established Pune OEM, and the used-car and service ecosystem.** Pune dealers report pre-owned bookings up 40% since last year on affordability and easy financing [2]. **So when an EV-bus proposal lands, check the PM-eBus Sewa payment-security cover and the actual registration share; if the borrower's share is small and receivables are from state transport undertakings, ask for the escrow or payment-security arrangement before sanctioning.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the order book, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock and receivable statements, a quarterly stock audit, and a covenant that receivables from any single OEM stay below an agreed share. **Take every month: the sales register, the top-five debtor ageing, and the inventory ageing.** Where the borrower is a supplier, insist on assignment of receivables or a tripartite arrangement with the OEM. **If the borrower is a used-car dealer, check the financing tie-up and the ticket size; if subvention is withdrawn, ask how the 40% booking growth [2] holds.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the receivable days and the inventory days together.** If receivable days stretch beyond the agreed limit for two months, cut the drawing power and ask for the OEM's payment confirmation. **If a supplier's order book falls while the OEM's output is rising, the borrower is losing share — ask for the latest purchase-order schedule.** On the EV side, if registrations do not track the claimed order book [1], treat the order book as unconfirmed.
